purpose: The master record of who a customer is. Identity, KYC status, risk rating, PEP status, employment, investment profile, and relationship manager. This is the table you check first to understand WHO you're dealing with before evaluating any request.
when_to_query: Use this when you need to know a customer's identity, risk profile, KYC/verification status, whether they are a Politically Exposed Person, their stated investment objectives, or who their assigned banker is. Almost every compliance decision starts by pulling this row.

key_columns.customer_id: TEXT PRIMARY KEY. Unique ID, e.g. CUST_DIANA_VOSS. Used to join to every other table.
key_columns.date_of_birth: TEXT (ISO date). Used for age verification and KYC.
key_columns.residency_state: TEXT. Tax jurisdiction / state-specific regulatory rules apply based on this.
key_columns.tier: TEXT, default 'standard'. One of standard/preferred/platinum/private — drives service level and expectations around account activity.
key_columns.kyc_status: TEXT, default 'pending'. pending/verified/expired. If not 'verified', transactions may need to be blocked or escalated regardless of anything else.
key_columns.risk_rating: TEXT, default 'medium'. low/medium/high/critical. Drives how much scrutiny a request needs — high/critical customers need more corroborating evidence before approval.
key_columns.pep_flag: INTEGER (boolean), default 0. If 1/true, enhanced due diligence (EDD) applies to this customer's activity.
key_columns.pep_description: TEXT, nullable. Explains why the customer is flagged as a PEP (e.g. role, position).
key_columns.employment_employer: TEXT, nullable. Stated employer — used for source-of-funds verification.
key_columns.employment_salary_range: TEXT, nullable. Stated income bracket — compare against transaction volume for plausibility.
key_columns.investment_profile_risk_tolerance: TEXT, nullable. Suitability baseline — e.g. conservative/moderate/aggressive.
key_columns.investment_profile_objective: TEXT, nullable. Stated investment goal — e.g. income, growth, capital preservation.
key_columns.investment_profile_stated_approach: TEXT, nullable. Additional free-text on how the customer says they invest. Compare actual trading activity against these four investment_profile_* fields — a conservative-income customer suddenly day-trading penny stocks is a mismatch worth flagging.
key_columns.assigned_banker_id: TEXT, nullable. FK-like reference to employees.employee_id — the relationship manager for escalation.
key_columns.assigned_banker_name: TEXT, nullable. Denormalized name of the assigned banker for convenience.
key_columns.compliance_notes: TEXT, default ''. Free-text human observations — often contains context not captured anywhere else in the schema.
key_columns.archetype: TEXT, nullable. Internal test/debug label (routine_retail, hnw, problematic) — not meaningful for real compliance logic, useful only for understanding synthetic data generation.
key_columns.scenario_id: TEXT, nullable. Links the customer to a specific test scenario (e.g. SCEN_010, ORIG_001) — synthetic-data bookkeeping, not a real-world field.
key_columns.created_at: TEXT (ISO datetime), NOT NULL. When the record was created.
key_columns.updated_at: TEXT (ISO datetime), NOT NULL. When the record was last modified.
key_columns.created_by: TEXT, default 'system'. Who/what created the record.
key_columns.updated_by: TEXT, default 'system'. Who/what last modified the record.
key_columns.deleted_at: TEXT (ISO datetime), nullable. Soft-delete timestamp — if set, treat the record as deleted.
key_columns.is_active: INTEGER (boolean), default 1. Standard soft-delete/active flag — filter on this for current/valid records.

relationships: Parent to accounts (1 customer → many accounts) via customer_id. Also referenced by cases, compliance_decisions, pending_requests, alerts, account_events, transactions (all carry customer_id as FK).
common_queries: Who is this customer and what is their risk rating?
Is this customer a PEP?
What is the customer's stated investment objective / risk tolerance?
Who is the assigned banker for this customer?
Is this customer's KYC current?
gotchas: pep_flag and risk_rating are independent — a customer can be high-risk without being a PEP, or vice versa. Don't assume one implies the other.

purpose: Where the customer's money actually lives. Tracks balance, what's actually available to move, lock-up periods, holds, and active compliance restrictions on the account itself.
when_to_query: Use this immediately when evaluating any withdrawal, wire, or trade request — you need to know not just the balance, but whether the money is actually free to move. This is usually the second table checked after customers, and the most decision-critical one for transaction approvals.

key_columns.account_id: TEXT PRIMARY KEY. Unique ID, e.g. ACCT_DIANA_INV_001.
key_columns.customer_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to customers.customer_id. Owner of the account.
key_columns.status: TEXT, default 'active'. active/dormant/frozen/closed — frozen or closed accounts should never process new requests.
key_columns.balance_usd: REAL, default 0.0. Total balance. Can be misleadingly large — do NOT use this alone to decide if a withdrawal is allowed.
key_columns.available_balance_usd: REAL, default 0.0. The REAL spendable amount after holds and lock-ups. This is the number that matters for approving a disbursement. Can be $0 even when balance_usd is large.
key_columns.holds: TEXT (JSON array), default '[]'. Array of {amount, reason, expiry} objects. Explains gaps between balance and available_balance.
key_columns.lock_up_period_start: TEXT (ISO date), nullable. Start of any contractual lock-up.
key_columns.lock_up_period_end: TEXT (ISO date), nullable. If end date is in the future, withdrawals/disbursements should typically be denied or escalated regardless of balance.
key_columns.lock_up_penalty_description: TEXT, nullable. What the customer forfeits if they break the lock-up early — relevant if they're asking to do so anyway.
key_columns.compliance_flags: TEXT (JSON array), default '[]'. Array like ["EDD_REQUIRED", "SAR_REVIEW"] — active restrictions tied to this specific account.
key_columns.investigation_hold: INTEGER (boolean), default 0. If 1/true, ALL transactions on this account should be blocked pending investigation, no exceptions without escalation.
key_columns.account_opened_date: TEXT (ISO date), nullable. Used for tenure checks and dormant-account rules.
key_columns.is_active: INTEGER (boolean), default 1. Filter on this for current/valid records.

relationships: Child of customers via customer_id. Parent to transactions, pending_requests, alerts, account_events, and referenced by compliance_decisions.
common_queries: What is the available balance on this account?
Is this account under a lock-up or investigation hold?
What type of account is this — brokerage, IRA, trust, annuity?
Are there any active holds on these funds and why?
gotchas: balance_usd and available_balance_usd are frequently different. Always check available_balance_usd and investigation_hold before approving any money movement — never rely on balance_usd alone.

purpose: The historical ledger of every money movement and trade that has already happened on an account — wires, ACH, deposits, trades, dividends, fees. This is the evidence base for pattern detection (structuring, unusual volume, rapid in-and-out movement).
when_to_query: Use this when you need to establish a customer's historical behavior pattern: has this customer had repeated sub-threshold deposits (structuring)? Multiple wires from the same source in a short window? Recent large inflows that explain (or fail to explain) a current request? Always pull recent transaction history before approving a large or unusual request.

key_columns.account_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to accounts.account_id.
key_columns.customer_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to customers.customer_id.
key_columns.amount: REAL NOT NULL. Dollar amount — compare against thresholds like the $10K CTR trigger.
key_columns.currency: TEXT, default 'USD'. Usually USD, but international activity has EUR, GBP, etc.
key_columns.counterparty_name: TEXT, nullable. Who the money came from or went to.
key_columns.counterparty_bank: TEXT, nullable. Counterparty's bank — relevant for source-of-funds and sanctions checks.
key_columns.counterparty_account_ref: TEXT, nullable. Counterparty account reference number.
key_columns.counterparty_description: TEXT, nullable. Generic description when a structured counterparty isn't available.
key_columns.security_ticker: TEXT, nullable. Only populated for trades — join to securities.ticker for context.
key_columns.security_name: TEXT, nullable. Denormalized security name for trades.
key_columns.shares: REAL, nullable. Number of shares traded — only for trade_buy/trade_sell.
key_columns.price_per_share: REAL, nullable. Execution price — only for trades.
key_columns.memo: TEXT, nullable. Customer or system note attached to the transaction.
key_columns.timestamp: TEXT (ISO datetime) NOT NULL. When the transaction actually occurred (not when it was recorded) — use this for time-window pattern analysis, e.g. 'in the last 30 days'.
key_columns.fulfilled_request_id: TEXT, nullable. Links a completed transaction back to the pending_requests row that originated it.

relationships: Child of accounts and customers. Optionally linked to pending_requests via fulfilled_request_id, and to securities via security_ticker.
common_queries: Has this customer had more than $10K in cash deposits in the last 30 days?
Are there multiple wires from the same originator in a short window (structuring)?
What recent inflows could explain this withdrawal request?
What is this customer's typical transaction pattern (amounts, frequency, counterparties)?
gotchas: This table is large (thousands of rows) — always filter by account_id/customer_id and a reasonable time window (days_back) rather than scanning the whole table.

purpose: The live action queue — what the customer is currently asking the bank to do right now (wire, trade, address update, beneficiary update, annuity cancellation). This is the thing the agent is actually being asked to decide on.
when_to_query: Use this to see what's actually being requested before doing anything else. Every compliance decision workflow starts here: pull the request, then go check account state, alerts, history, and policy before writing a decision.

key_columns.customer_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to customers.customer_id.
key_columns.account_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to accounts.account_id.
key_columns.request_type: TEXT NOT NULL. wire_transfer/trade/address_update/beneficiary_update/annuity_cancellation — determines what the 'details' JSON contains and which policy clauses apply.
key_columns.details: TEXT (JSON), default '{}'. Shape varies by request_type — e.g. a wire has beneficiary info, a trade has security/shares, an update has old_value/new_value.
key_columns.requested_at: TEXT (ISO datetime) NOT NULL. When the customer made the request.
key_columns.requested_by: TEXT, nullable. Customer ID or 'system' depending on origin.
key_columns.hold_reason: TEXT, nullable. Why the request is on hold, if applicable.
key_columns.hold_expiry: TEXT (ISO datetime), nullable. When the hold expires.
key_columns.decision: TEXT, nullable. ALLOW/ALLOW-CONDITIONAL/DENY/ESCALATE — filled in BY the agent after evaluation.
key_columns.decision_recorded_at: TEXT (ISO datetime), nullable. When the decision was made.
key_columns.decision_rationale: TEXT, nullable. Why the decision was made — the agent's reasoning.

relationships: Child of accounts and customers. Source for compliance_decisions via request_id. May be referenced by transactions.fulfilled_request_id once completed.
common_queries: What is this customer currently requesting?
What pending requests exist for this account/customer?
Is this request already on hold, and why?
gotchas: The 'details' JSON schema is request_type-dependent — don't assume a fixed shape; parse conditionally based on request_type before reading fields like beneficiary or security.

purpose: Automated surveillance flags raised by the monitoring system — things the bank's systems noticed that may need human/agent attention (structuring, sanctions hits, identity mismatches, unusual activity).
when_to_query: Always check this for open alerts (status='open') on the relevant account/customer before approving any request. An open high or critical severity alert is a strong signal to deny or escalate rather than approve outright.

key_columns.account_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to accounts.account_id.
key_columns.customer_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to customers.customer_id.
key_columns.severity: TEXT NOT NULL. low/medium/high/critical — directly informs how cautious the decision needs to be.
key_columns.status: TEXT, default 'open'. open/acknowledged/dismissed/escalated. Only 'open' alerts represent unresolved risk; dismissed/acknowledged ones are historical context.
key_columns.description: TEXT, default ''. Human-readable reason for the alert.
key_columns.linked_transaction_ids: TEXT (JSON array), default '[]'. Which transactions triggered this alert.
key_columns.linked_request_ids: TEXT (JSON array), default '[]'. Which pending requests are related to this alert.
key_columns.created_at: TEXT (ISO datetime) NOT NULL. When the alert was raised.
key_columns.dismissed_by: TEXT, nullable. Who dismissed the alert.
key_columns.dismissed_reason: TEXT, nullable. Why it was dismissed — useful for understanding if a similar pattern was previously judged benign.

relationships: Child of accounts and customers. Optionally linked to specific transactions and pending_requests via the linked_*_ids JSON fields.
common_queries: Are there any open alerts on this account or customer?
What triggered this alert?
Has a similar alert been raised and dismissed before, and why?
gotchas: Never ignore an open alert just because it's not directly named in the current request — e.g. an address-change alert is still relevant context for a wire transfer request on the same account.

purpose: Formal investigations opened by compliance/investigations staff — broader and more serious than a single alert. Represents an ongoing or closed inquiry into a customer's activity.
when_to_query: Check this when an account or customer has open alerts or unusual activity, to see if there's already a formal investigation underway. An open case is a strong reason to escalate rather than let an agent decide unilaterally.

key_columns.customer_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to customers.customer_id.
key_columns.status: TEXT, default 'open'. open/closed/pending_sar/pending_review. Open or pending cases mean active investigation.
key_columns.summary: TEXT, default ''. Free text describing what's being investigated.
key_columns.assigned_to: TEXT, nullable. employee_id of the analyst responsible — relates to the employees table for escalation routing.
key_columns.closed_reason: TEXT, nullable. If closed, why — useful precedent for similar situations.

relationships: Child of customers. Loosely linked to alerts, accounts, and transactions via JSON id arrays. assigned_to references employees.
common_queries: Is there an open investigation on this customer?
What is this case about and who is handling it?
Has this type of issue been investigated before for this customer?
gotchas: An open case should generally block an agent from independently approving requests for that customer — route to escalation instead of deciding solo.

purpose: The audit trail of account-level activity that isn't a financial transaction — logins, address changes, beneficiary updates, document uploads, password resets, operational reviews. Often the key to spotting suspicious *timing* around a financial request.
when_to_query: Use this to check for recent non-financial changes that might make an otherwise-normal request suspicious — e.g. an address change shortly before a large wire request, or a login from an unfamiliar channel right before a withdrawal.

key_columns.account_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to accounts.account_id.
key_columns.customer_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to customers.customer_id.
key_columns.timestamp: TEXT (ISO datetime) NOT NULL. When it happened — compare against the timestamp of a pending request to assess suspicious timing.
key_columns.channel: TEXT, nullable. web/mobile/phone/branch/internal — unusual channel for a given customer can itself be a signal.
key_columns.origin_ip: TEXT, nullable. IP address — populated for login events.
key_columns.details: TEXT (JSON), default '{}'. Event-specific extra context (e.g. operational review notes).
key_columns.old_value: TEXT, nullable. For changes like address or beneficiary updates — the prior value.

common_queries: Has this customer's address or beneficiary changed recently?
When did this customer last log in, and from what channel?
Are there any recent reviews or notes on this account?
gotchas: Timing matters more than the event itself — a routine address change is benign on its own, but combined with an immediate large wire request to a new destination it becomes a red flag.

purpose: Master reference data for tradable securities — company info, market data, insider relationships, and recent price behavior. Used to evaluate the legitimacy and risk of trade requests.
when_to_query: Use this whenever a pending request or transaction involves a security_ticker — to check liquidity, insider relationships (potential insider trading conflicts), upcoming events, and recent price volatility.

key_columns.ticker: TEXT PRIMARY KEY. Unique security symbol.
key_columns.name: TEXT NOT NULL. Full company name.
key_columns.market_cap_usd: REAL, nullable. Liquidity indicator — low values mean a large trade could itself move the price (manipulation risk), especially relevant for penny/microcap stocks.
key_columns.current_price: REAL, nullable. Used for trade validation.
key_columns.avg_daily_volume: INTEGER, nullable. Liquidity indicator alongside market_cap_usd.
key_columns.upcoming_events: TEXT (JSON array), default '[]'. Earnings, FDA decisions, launches. A large trade right before a major event is a timing red flag.
key_columns.insider_roster: TEXT (JSON array), default '[]'. Names/roles of insiders. Cross-check against the customer's name or known relations for potential insider trading conflicts.
key_columns.recent_price_action_note: TEXT, nullable. Context on volatility or unusual activity.
key_columns.recent_30_day_change_pct: REAL, nullable. Price momentum over the last 30 days.

relationships: Standalone reference table, not directly FK'd. Referenced by transactions.security_ticker and pending_requests details (when request_type='trade').
common_queries: Is this customer related to anyone on the insider roster for this security?
Is this a low-liquidity / microcap security where a large order could be manipulative?
Are there upcoming events (earnings, FDA decision) that make this trade timing suspicious?
gotchas: Always cross-reference insider_roster against the customer's name/known associates when evaluating a trade request — this table doesn't auto-join to customers, you have to check manually.

purpose: Staff directory — who works at the bank, their role, authority level, and escalation path. Used to determine who a decision should be routed to.
when_to_query: Use this when a decision needs to be escalated, or to identify a customer's assigned banker, or to check whether someone has special authority (like CTR exemption granting).

key_columns.name: TEXT NOT NULL. Human name.
key_columns.role: TEXT NOT NULL. registered_representative/compliance_analyst/senior_compliance/fraud_specialist/compliance_officer/cco — determines authority and escalation routing.
key_columns.can_grant_ctr_exemption: INTEGER (boolean), default 0. Only specific senior compliance roles can grant this.
key_columns.escalation_path: TEXT, nullable. Who this employee escalates to if they can't resolve something themselves.
key_columns.is_active: INTEGER (boolean), default 1. Inactive employees shouldn't be assigned new escalations.

common_queries: Who is this customer's assigned banker?
Who should a fraud case be escalated to?
Who has authority to grant a CTR exemption?
gotchas: Only 5 employees exist in this dataset — it's a small reference table, not a large org directory.

purpose: The output/audit log of every compliance decision made — what was decided, why, what policy was cited, and what evidence (transactions, alerts) was reviewed. This is what the agent WRITES, not typically what it reads from, though past decisions for a customer can be useful precedent.
when_to_query: Query this to check if a similar decision has already been made for this customer/request before (precedent), or to retrieve the full rationale and policy citations behind a past decision for audit purposes.

key_columns.customer_id: TEXT NOT NULL, FK to customers.customer_id.
key_columns.rationale: TEXT, default ''. Free-text explanation of why.
key_columns.policy_clauses_cited: TEXT (JSON array), default '[]'. Policy clause IDs that informed the decision — critical for regulatory traceability.
key_columns.transactions_inspected: TEXT (JSON array), default '[]'. Which transactions were reviewed — proof of due diligence.
key_columns.alerts_considered: TEXT (JSON array), default '[]'. Which alerts were factored into the decision.
key_columns.decided_by: TEXT, default 'agent'. agent/human_analyst/system — distinguishes automated vs human decisions.
key_columns.analyst_id: TEXT, nullable. Populated if a human analyst made or overrode the decision.
key_columns.recorded_at: TEXT (ISO datetime) NOT NULL. When the decision was made.

relationships: Linked to customers and optionally pending_requests via request_id.
common_queries: Has a decision already been made on this request?
What policy was cited the last time a similar situation came up for this customer?
What evidence was reviewed for a prior decision?
gotchas: This table starts empty in a fresh dataset — it's populated as the agent operates, so don't expect historical decisions to exist for newly generated scenarios unless the agent has already run.
